doc.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: Analyzing the Extension melody and voice leading
summary: Dobbins explains how the inner voice makes the blues melody work.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: it was I guess one of the things that threw me off. Because the melody is real simple too. It’s a B flat blues and has lots of minor thirds [plays piano], then it goes to the four [plays piano], and then to one [plays piano] and then to five [plays piano] and then one again before it hits the tonic, which has the fifth in the melody or no, the third in the melody [plays piano]. That’s how it ends. But when I tried to put that melody with the chords, one of the things that started giving me trouble was when I put the melody with the chords it didn’t seem to work [plays piano]. Especially with this chord [plays piano]. [inaudible] it was the saxophones, it was that second voice that made everything work [plays piano]. Now that’s unresolved, but listen to what happens at the end of the next phrase [inaudible]. Then it resolves [plays piano]. And along the way you’ve got all these things. It starts with a G7, with the 4th in the melody, against the 3rd. With that A flat it softens them both because it makes consonant intervals. A major 6th, a major 3rd. It’s just enough to — and the next chord is C7 but it’s got this note [plays piano]. Once again, you know, you’ve got this consonance that’s taking some of your attention away from that. And eventually when you get to the end of the phrase [plays piano] it gets to the third. This voice — not yet, but the next time you get there [plays piano]. So that’s this thing I was talking about before, of that real musicians that really hear music as language, the way other people use words but in relation to a really specific language, when they introduce a dissonance, whether it’s in the melody or in an inner voice in the harmony, it’s there for a reason. And if you listen to it and pay attention to it, you’ll eventually hear why they did that. Because it ends up going there.
There’s a whole lesson there for arrangers and composers.
Yeah. And the thing that relates to improvising then is I started realizing like if you take, one of the things that Clare uses actually comes from —
